units.title: Test levels, oracles, boundary cases and test doubles
outcomes: Distinguish unit, contract, integration, end-to-end and performance tests by the failure each can detect.
Turn a requirement into an invariant, an independent oracle, representative examples and boundary cases.
Build a pytest suite with fixtures, parametrization and test doubles that has no order dependence.
units.why: Most ML bugs hide at component boundaries, not inside one function. The test level decides which failures you can see, and the oracle decides whether the test checks anything at all.

next.note: Generalize example tests into properties with generated inputs.
Pin fixed behavior as regression tests and isolate nondeterminism.

study.locator: Testing: unit, integration and functional tests, test-driven development, regression tests, property-based tests and mocks; Code coverage

focus: Each level detects a different failure: unit tests catch logic errors in one function, contract tests catch seam drift, integration tests catch wiring errors, end-to-end tests catch requirement misses.
An oracle must be independent of the code under test: a reimplementation, the standard library, a known value or a metamorphic relation. Asserting code output against itself proves nothing.
Boundary cases carry the failures: empty input, single element, duplicates, limits and malformed rows. Parametrize them explicitly.
Function scope is the default for a reason: shared mutable fixtures create order dependence. Use yield fixtures for teardown and monkeypatch for automatic undo.
units.reproduce: From a blank directory, write a small parsing module and a pytest file with one parametrized boundary test, one yield fixture using tmp_path, and one monkeypatched environment test. Run pytest and get 5 passed in about 0.3 s on a 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K with Python 3.14.4 and pytest 9.1.1.
traps: Mocking the unit you should be testing. Mock at the seam you do not own, such as network, clock or filesystem, and keep one contract test that touches the real dependency.
Module- or session-scoped mutable fixtures. Tests pass alone and fail together; keep shared fixtures immutable or hand out fresh copies from a factory.
Reading 100 percent line coverage as correctness. Coverage shows which lines ran, not which requirements were checked, so the lecture warns against over-indexing on it.

selfTest.q: A function returns correct values but writes rows the loader cannot read. Which test level catches this?
selfTest.a: An integration or contract test at the writer and loader seam. A unit test of either side alone passes.

selfTest.q: Why is asserting your sort equals your second sort implementation weak, and what is stronger?
selfTest.a: Both can share your misunderstanding. A stronger oracle is independent: the standard library sorted, a fixed fixture, or a property such as the output being ordered.

selfTest.q: Two tests share a module-scoped dict fixture and pass alone but fail together. What is wrong?
selfTest.a: One test mutates shared state the other reads. Make the fixture function-scoped or return a fresh copy per test.

selfTest.q: monkeypatch.setenv in one test changes a later test. How is that possible?
selfTest.a: It is not, if monkeypatch was used: pytest undoes every monkeypatch change at teardown. A leak means the test wrote to os.environ directly.

practice.locator: Exercises, item 2: write a unit test for a project, generate an HTML coverage report and inspect uncovered lines
practice.note: Apply it to the parsing module from Reproduce and add one boundary test for each uncovered line the report shows.

units.stopWhen: Your five-test suite passes, every test also passes alone by node id, and you can name the oracle and the boundary behind each assertion.

fit.note: The lecture plus the pytest fixture and monkeypatch guides cover all three topics at explain and implement depth, with a named coverage exercise for practice.

units.title: Property, metamorphic and differential testing with shrinking
outcomes: State a property, metamorphic relation or differential oracle for a small function and encode it with Hypothesis strategies.
Read a shrunk counterexample and turn it into a minimal permanent regression case.
Replay persisted failures from the example database and pin them with @example instead of opaque blobs.
units.why: Examples check the inputs you thought of. Properties check the inputs you did not, and shrinking hands you the smallest case that breaks your claim.

next.note: Treat nondeterministic property failures as flakiness to isolate, not to rerun.
Feed shrunk counterexamples into a hypothesis log as the first observation.

study.locator: Install Hypothesis through Write your first test; Running in a test suite; the max_examples default of 100

study.title: Hypothesis strategies reference
study.locator: Primitives, Numeric and Collections: integers, text and lists, and combining them

study.title: Hypothesis test settings
study.locator: Changing the number of test cases; Changing settings across your test suite with profiles

study.title: Replaying failed Hypothesis tests
study.locator: The Hypothesis database; Using @example to run a specific input; Replaying test cases with @reproduce_failure; Prefer @example over the database for correctness

focus: A property relates many inputs to expected structure: ordered output, round trips, idempotence. A metamorphic relation compares outputs across related inputs; a differential test compares two implementations on the same inputs.
Strategies generate the inputs, and only the draw sequence plus the outcome must stay deterministic. Randomness, clocks and global state inside the test break replay.
Shrinking minimizes the failing case automatically. The report shows the minimal input, not the first one found.
The database replays past failures before generating new ones. Pin durable cases with @example; a @reproduce_failure blob is opaque and version-fragile, so convert it promptly.
units.reproduce: Run a @given(st.integers(min_value=0)) test asserting n < 50 with max_examples=200 and derandomize=True: it fails and reports n=50, the minimal failure, in well under a second on a 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K with Python 3.14.4 and Hypothesis 6.169.0. Run it again and watch it fail instantly from the .hypothesis database. Then assert sorted(sorted(xs)) == sorted(xs) over st.lists(st.integers()) and see 200 examples pass.
traps: Filtering with plain if inside the test instead of assume or constrained strategies. Rejected examples slow generation and can trip the data_too_large health check.
Keeping a @reproduce_failure blob as the regression test. It is opaque and may stop replaying after upgrades, so rewrite it as @example.
Calling a nondeterministic property suite green. A flaky failure poisons the database, so fix determinism first.

selfTest.q: Hypothesis tried a large integer first but reports n=50. Why?
selfTest.a: Shrinking. After finding a failure it searches for the smallest input that still fails, so the report shows the minimal case.

selfTest.q: When should a failing case live in @example rather than the database?
selfTest.a: Always for durable regressions. The database replays automatically but can invalidate across versions, while @example runs every time in the explicit phase.

selfTest.q: Give a metamorphic relation for a serializer plus parser pair.
selfTest.a: parse(serialize(tree)) equals tree for every generated tree. It relates two outputs without needing an independent oracle.

selfTest.q: A property test fails only on some runs of identical code. What must you check?
selfTest.a: Determinism of draws plus outcome: unmanaged randomness, time, filesystem or global state. Only that sequence needs to be deterministic.

practice.note: Run it, read the shrunk n=50 report, then convert the case to @example.

units.title: Regression tests, failure injection and flaky tests
outcomes: Write a regression test that fails on the old code and passes on the fix, and mark known-bad behavior with strict xfail.
Inject a targeted fault, such as a full disk or a failing dependency, and show the suite catching it.
Measure a flake rate, isolate its randomness, time, concurrency or state source, and quarantine deliberately instead of rerunning blindly.
units.why: A fixed bug returns unless a test pins it. A flaky test teaches the team to ignore red builds, which hides the next real failure.

next.note: Turn the isolated flake or regression into a hypothesis log with tool evidence.
Bisect the history to find which commit introduced the regression.

study.locator: Skipping test functions and skipif; XFail with condition, reason, raises, run and strict parameters; Skip/xfail with parametrize

study.title: pytest flaky tests explanation
study.locator: Why flaky tests are a problem; Potential root causes: system state, overly strict assertion and thread safety; Other general strategies: split up test suites and quarantine

study.title: Hypothesis flaky failures
study.locator: Common sources of flakiness; Types of flakiness: Flaky failure and Flaky strategy definition

study.title: Reproducing resource issues
study.locator: Watching and reproducing resource issues: emulating an almost full disk and exhausted CPU memory

focus: A regression test names the defect: it fails before the fix and passes after. Write it before the fix when you can.
xfail with strict=True turns an unexpected pass into a failure, so fixed bugs announce themselves. Unstrict xfail as permanent quarantine is dangerous; the pytest guide says so.
Flakiness means uncontrolled state: randomness, clocks, threads, leftover files or test order. Parallel runs and randomized ordering expose order dependence.
Rerun plugins and quarantines mitigate; they do not fix. Isolate the source first, then control it, quarantine it with an owner, or delete the test.
units.reproduce: Write assert random.random() < 0.5 and run it 10 times: expect about half to fail (5 failed and 5 passed here, about 0.07 s per run on a 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K with Python 3.14.4 and pytest 9.1.1). Seed random with a fixed seed and run 5 times for 5 passed. Then mark a known failure xfail(strict=True), fix the code, and watch the suite fail on XPASS until you remove the mark.
traps: Rerunning the suite until green and merging. The team learns to distrust failures, so quarantine with a ticket instead.
xfail without strict on a fixed bug. The suite stays green while the mark silently goes stale.
Wall-clock sleeps as synchronization. Load makes them flaky, so wait on events or poll with deadlines instead.

selfTest.q: A test fails one run in twenty. What is the first measurement, and what comes after?
selfTest.a: The flake rate over repeated runs, then isolation: seed randomness, fix clocks, serialize threads, clean state, and run the test alone versus in the suite.

selfTest.q: When is strict xfail the right tool?
selfTest.a: A known bug with a test: the suite stays green while it fails and goes red with XPASS when fixed, which forces removal of the mark.

selfTest.q: A test passes alone but fails under parallel workers. What does that suggest?
selfTest.a: Order dependence or shared state: a previous test leaves data behind, or the test needs data another test creates.

selfTest.q: Why does pytest.approx belong in a flake fix for float asserts?
selfTest.a: Exact float equality is an overly strict assertion: tiny representation differences fail otherwise identical runs. approx compares within tolerance.

units.stopWhen: You can quote the flake rate before and after your fix, the regression test fails on the old code, and no test needs a rerun to pass.

units.title: Debuggers, logs, traces and competing hypotheses
outcomes: Rank competing root-cause hypotheses and pick the observation that distinguishes them before editing code.
Drive pdb, logging, strace and sanitizer output to locate a defect with tool evidence.
Shrink a failure to a minimal reproducer and pin it with a regression test.
units.why: Editing before observing creates new bugs while the old one hides. A short hypothesis log plus one distinguishing observation usually beats an hour of guessing.

next.note: Diagnose processes from the shell with streams, exit status, signals and strace.
Bisect the history once the log points at a recent change.

focus: Write two or three competing hypotheses first, each with the single observation that would kill it. Run the cheapest distinguishing observation before changing code.
Confirm you run the code you edit: check the module path for installed copies shadowing the repo. Every later observation misleads otherwise.

Match the tool to the question: breakpoint for state, logging for history, strace -f -e trace=file for missing files and hangs, AddressSanitizer for memory corruption, rr reverse-continue for Heisenbugs.
On Python 3.14, python -m pdb -p PID attaches to a running process. For a hard hang, py-spy dump needs no cooperation from the target.
units.reproduce: Seed an off-by-one in a function you tested in the first unit. Write three competing hypotheses with their killing observations in a log file. Confirm the import path, set one breakpoint, read the distinguishing variable, fix, and add the regression test. End state: the log shows each rejected hypothesis with its evidence, and the suite is green.
traps: Debugging the wrong copy: an installed package shadows your edited repo file. Check the module path before trusting any observation.
Observing with prints that change timing. Race bugs vanish under prints, so use rr recording or strace instead.
Declaring victory without a regression test. The next refactor reintroduces the same defect silently.

selfTest.q: Two hypotheses: wrong constant versus wrong index. What is one distinguishing observation?
selfTest.a: Break at the indexing line and read the index and the constant. One read kills one hypothesis.

selfTest.q: A program hangs on startup with no output. Which tool first, and with what flags?
selfTest.a: strace -f -e trace=file, or plain strace. It shows the last system call, often a blocked read on a missing file or socket, without touching the code.

selfTest.q: Why convert prints to log statements after the fix?
selfTest.a: Logs keep severity, destination and history for the next similar bug. Removed prints lose the evidence path; the lecture recommends this explicitly.

selfTest.q: rr records a passing run of a race bug. What now?
selfTest.a: Record again until a failing run is captured: rr serializes scheduling, so intermittent races may need several attempts. Then replay deterministically with reverse debugging.

units.title: Shell streams, exit status, signals, processes and permissions
outcomes: Write a fail-fast script that quotes paths, validates inputs, propagates exit status and cleans up on signals.
Diagnose a failed process from exit status, streams, permissions, environment and signal behavior.
Explain quoting, redirection, pipelines, job control and partial-output recovery without trial and error.
units.why: Every experiment runs through a shell. An unquoted path or a swallowed exit code turns a clean failure into silent corruption.

next.note: Run the same fail-fast scripts on remote hosts over SSH inside tmux.
Use strace and process state as debugger evidence for hangs and missing files.

study.title: Bash execution control and background logs
study.locator: Bash: Controlling script execution with set -e, -u, -o pipefail and -x traces; nohup and log redirection

focus: Quote every expansion and keep globs unquoted only when intended. Single quotes preserve literally; double quotes allow expansion.
Use set -euo pipefail plus a trap that cleans up on EXIT, INT and TERM. Without pipefail, false | true exits 0 and the failure vanishes.
Streams are separate contracts: stdout carries data, stderr carries diagnostics, the exit code carries the outcome. Redirect and check each one deliberately.
Background jobs report through $!, wait and kill. Partial output stays recoverable when each stage writes its own log.
units.reproduce: Write check-and-run.sh with a shebang, set -euo pipefail, a quoted $1 filename check with test -f, a trap that removes its temp file, and separate stdout and stderr logs. Show that false | true exits 1 under pipefail and 0 without it on GNU bash 5.3.9, and that SIGTERM still removes the temp file with exit code 143.
traps: set -e does not fire inside if conditions, && lists, or pipelines without pipefail. Test failure handling explicitly instead of assuming strictness.
Unquoted variables and command substitutions split on spaces. Filenames with spaces become several arguments, so quote or use arrays.
Reading $? after another command. Capture it immediately, because any intervening command overwrites it.

selfTest.q: false | true; echo $? prints what with and without pipefail?
selfTest.a: 1 with pipefail, 0 without. The pipeline status is the last command unless pipefail propagates the failure.

selfTest.q: Why must cd be a shell builtin?
selfTest.a: A child process cannot change its parent working directory, so cd must run in the shell itself.

selfTest.q: A script cleans up on Ctrl-C but not on kill -9. Why?
selfTest.a: SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored. Traps handle INT and TERM but never KILL, so temp files must tolerate it.

selfTest.q: Output still appears after cmd 2>/dev/null. What happened?
selfTest.a: The redirect applied to only one pipeline stage, or the message comes from the shell itself. Redirect each stage or the command group.

units.title: Git history, merges, rebases, bisect and recovery
outcomes: Explain commits, branches, merges, rebases and detached state using the snapshot graph.
Isolate a regression with bisect run from an automated failing test.
Recover a displaced commit with reflog without discarding unrelated work.
units.why: History is the experiment log of the code. Bisect finds which change broke behavior, and reflog makes almost every Git mistake reversible.

next.note: Version releases and lockfiles on top of a disciplined history.
Bisect feeds the hypothesis log once it points at a recent change.

study.title: Pro Git: undoing and data recovery
study.locator: Maintenance and Data Recovery: Data Recovery; for everyday undo, read Undoing Things with git restore at https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Undoing-Things first

focus: A commit is a snapshot plus parents, and a branch is a movable pointer. Merge preserves both parents; rebase rewrites commits onto a new base.
Rebase only local, unpushed work. Rebasing pushed history forces everyone downstream to repair, which the book states as the rule.
Bisect needs a monotonic test: nonzero exit on bad, zero on good, plus one known-good and one known-bad commit. git bisect run automates the search in logarithmic steps.
Recovery is preservation-first: stash or branch current state before any destructive command. Uncommitted work is invisible to reflog, and unreachable entries expire after 30 days by default.
units.reproduce: Build a 7-commit repo with a regression in commit 6 and a test.sh that exits 1 on the bad line. Run git bisect start, bad, good HEAD~6 and run ./test.sh: it reports commit 6 as the first bad commit in 2 steps. Then delete a branch tip and recover it with git reflog plus git branch recovered <sha>. Observed with git 2.51.0.
traps: Destructive commands before saving state. Uncommitted work never reaches the reflog, so stash or commit before reset --hard or clean.
Bisecting with a flaky or non-monotonic test. The search converges on the wrong commit, so stabilize the test first.
Rebasing a shared branch then force-pushing. Use merge, or rebase only with coordination, and never rewrite pushed history silently.

selfTest.q: Merge versus rebase for a finished feature branch: what differs in the graph?
selfTest.a: Merge adds a merge commit with two parents and preserves branch history. Rebase replays the branch commits onto the main tip as new hashes with a linear history.

selfTest.q: git bisect run reports the wrong culprit. Name two causes.
selfTest.a: A flaky non-monotonic test, or a bad and good labeling error. Uncommitted changes skewing some checkouts is a third.

selfTest.q: You deleted a branch yesterday and need its tip. What is the exact recovery?
selfTest.a: git reflog, find the tip sha, then git branch recovered <sha>. It works while the reflog entry survives expiry.

selfTest.q: In detached HEAD state, what does committing do, and what is the risk?
selfTest.a: The commit exists but no branch points at it. Switching away strands it except in the reflog, so create a branch to keep it.

outcomes: Create ed25519 keys, configure hosts, copy keys and disable password authentication.
Forward a remote port to localhost and run it in the background without secrets in logs.
Run a task in a named tmux session that survives disconnects and reattach cleanly.
units.why: Remote machines do the heavy work. Keys plus tmux turn a fragile connection into a durable session with no password typed twice.

next.note: Run clean-environment builds on the remote host you can now reach reliably.
Supervise remote services beyond a personal tmux session.

study.locator: Remote Machines: ssh invocation, key generation with ssh-keygen -a 100 -t ed25519, ssh-copy-id, ~/.ssh/config entries and LocalForward; Exercises under Remote Machines (SSH)

study.locator: Terminal Multiplexers: tmux sessions, detaching and reattaching, windows and panes; Exercises under Terminal Multiplexers

focus: Host trust and user trust are different files: known_hosts authenticates the server, authorized_keys authenticates you. Read first-connection prompts instead of reflex-typing yes.
One key per client, passphrase protected, loaded in the agent. The private key never leaves the client; copy the .pub with ssh-copy-id.
LocalForward exposes a remote port locally, and -N -f backgrounds the tunnel. Never paste tokens or keys into commands that land in shell history or logs.
tmux owns the session, not the correctness. Name sessions, detach with the prefix plus d, reattach with tmux a -t. A dead server still kills the session.
units.reproduce: Generate ssh-keygen -a 100 -t ed25519 demokey and get demokey plus demokey.pub. Add a Host vm entry with HostName, User and IdentityFile, then verify with ssh -G vm that hostname, user, port and identityfile resolve (observed with OpenSSH 10.2). Then run tmux new -d -s atlas, tmux ls, detach, reattach and kill-session (observed with tmux 3.6a).
traps: Agent forwarding to untrusted hosts. A root user on the remote can use your agent, so forward only where needed and prefer ProxyJump.
Leaving password authentication enabled. Keys plus disabled passwords close brute force; the exercises walk through sshd_config.
Treating tmux as supervision. It survives disconnects, not reboots or out-of-memory kills; real services need a supervisor.

selfTest.q: known_hosts versus authorized_keys: who trusts whom?
selfTest.a: known_hosts on the client records server keys, so the client trusts the server. authorized_keys on the server records client keys, so the server trusts the client.

selfTest.q: What does LocalForward 9999 localhost:8888 in Host vm do?
selfTest.a: Connections to local port 9999 travel through the SSH link to vm and emerge as connections to its localhost:8888.

selfTest.q: SSH drops mid-run inside tmux. What survives?
selfTest.a: The tmux server and its processes keep running. Reattach to see the output intact. Anything outside tmux got SIGHUP unless started with nohup.

selfTest.q: Why is ssh -N -f useful for forwarding, and what do the flags do?
selfTest.a: -N runs no remote command and -f backgrounds after authentication: a quiet tunnel with no shell.

focus: Applications pin, libraries range. uv.lock records exact versions with hashes, and CI enforces it with uv sync --locked.
A manifest names everything the run needs: commit sha, config, data checksum, seed, environment lock and output hash. Diff the manifest, not memories.
Gates run in order of cost: format, lint, typecheck, fast tests, build, clean-environment install. Pre-commit runs the cheap ones locally; CI runs all of them.
Hermetic builds pin the toolchain too, for bit-identical artifacts. Reach for Nix or Bazel only when lockfiles plus containers still diverge.
units.reproduce: Run uv init plus uv lock on a fresh package and get a uv.lock with version = 1 and the project entry (observed resolving 1 package with uv 0.11.32). Create a venv, diff printenv before and after, and see VIRTUAL_ENV and VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT appear with python resolving inside the venv.
traps: Committing the venv or resolving unlocked in CI. The lock only reproduces when CI enforces --locked.
Pinning == in a reusable library. Your pin becomes every downstream conflict, so range the library and pin the app.
CI that tests the working tree but never installs the built wheel. Packaging bugs ship green, so add a clean-install smoke step.

selfTest.q: uv.lock exists but CI runs uv sync without --locked. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The resolver may pick newer versions satisfying the pyproject ranges, so the run no longer matches the lock. --locked fails instead of drifting.

selfTest.q: Why does the lecture recommend ranges for libraries and pins for apps?
selfTest.a: Libraries compose with other dependencies, so strict pins conflict. Apps are final consumers, so exact pins give every run identical inputs.

selfTest.q: A manifest lists code sha, config, data checksum, seed, lockfile hash and output hash. Identical code gives a different output: where do you look?
selfTest.a: The config, data, seed and environment entries. The manifest turns same code with different results into a named diff.

selfTest.q: Pre-commit passes but CI fails on lint. What usually differs?
selfTest.a: Versions or scope: hooks pinned differently from CI, or CI checks files the hooks skip. Pin the same tool versions in both.
